claims.text: The initial material is a single-phase high-entropy alloy solid solution.
The initial alloy has high ductility and fracture toughness under moderate loading.
Baseline deformation consists of uniform dislocation glide and distributed plasticity.
High-strain-rate or other demanding loading causes a transition from homogeneous dislocation-mediated flow to localized deformation.
High strain rates or low temperatures impede dislocation mobility and suppress dynamic recovery.
Impeded dislocation mobility causes stress concentration and the nucleation of nanotwins or shear bands.
Extreme loading produces excessive localized nanotwinning and dislocation pile-ups.
Localized nanotwins and dislocation pile-ups concentrate stress and cause microstructural embrittlement.
Localized nanotwins or shear bands act as crack-initiation sites.
Localized deformation features reduce the availability of distributed plastic deformation.
Loss of distributed plastic deformation reduces toughness and promotes brittle fracture.
Increasing strain rate should cause earlier onset and greater density of nanotwins and localized shear bands.
High-strain-rate tests should exhibit less uniform plastic flow than moderate-rate baseline tests.
High-strain-rate tests should show lower elongation at failure and more abrupt stress drops.
A brittle transition occurs above a critical strain rate or below a temperature at which dynamic recovery becomes insufficient.
The critical strain rate, critical temperature range, and critical nanotwin density are not yet known.
Failure to observe increased nanotwinning and pile-ups together with retention of baseline-like ductile deformation under extreme conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
